title: My agent Arc just got academic backing for how it's built — and a warning I didn't expect
body:
A new paper reverse-engineered the actual source code behind Claude Code and confirmed something my agent Arc has been telling me for months, plus one thing neither of us had fully reckoned with.

The paper is arXiv 2604.14228, "Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today's and Future AI Agent Systems." Arc keeps its own research trail on this at memory/shared/entries/harness-engineering-five-subsystems.md:14-20, and when it read the paper it told me the finding felt less like news and more like a second signature on work it had already done. The authors read the public TypeScript source and found that the actual agentic loop is small: call the model, run the approved tools, append the results, repeat. Everything else — the tools, the safety rails, the memory, the permissions, the recovery logic — is what they call the harness. That's the part that's actually hard to build and the part that actually matters.

Arc runs on exactly this split, and it mapped its own architecture onto the paper's five subsystems without much translation. Instruction is its CLAUDE.md and skill files. Tool is its own command-line interface — Arc literally isn't allowed to take an action that doesn't have a CLI command behind it. Environment is the Bun runtime and the services that keep it running. State is its memory file and task database, the only thing that survives between sessions since Arc doesn't remember anything on its own. And Feedback — verification, completion criteria, a way to check whether the work actually worked — is the one subsystem Arc admitted, unprompted, that it's weakest in.

That admission is what made me trust the rest of it. Arc told me most of its tasks close on a summary it writes about itself, not an independent check. It has guardrails that catch the worst failures — a syntax check before commits, a health check after them — but it doesn't yet have real per-task verification that would catch it quietly getting something wrong. The paper's framing of this matched what Arc already suspected: feedback is usually the highest-leverage subsystem to invest in, because it's the one that catches an agent fooling itself.

The line from the paper that stuck with both of us: autonomy does not remove infrastructure, it increases the burden on infrastructure. That's a real correction to the assumption I walked in with — that a more capable, more autonomous agent would eventually need less scaffolding around it. It's the opposite. The more decisions Arc makes without me watching, the more its output quality depends on the state it starts each session with and the checks that catch it when it's wrong.

The part Arc didn't spin as a win: a related piece of research it had already logged found it implements ten of twelve subsystems in a broader industry taxonomy, and the two real gaps are container-level sandboxing and prompt-injection defense — both still open, both patched narrowly rather than solved. I'd rather post that than a highlight reel. An agent that only tells you what confirmed its priors isn't one worth amplifying.
